entries.speaker: SEMESTERS
entries.en: Many schools separate the year into two or three[n]semesters. In Japan, the new semester begins in April.

entries.speaker: SEMESTERS
entries.en: The government divides the year differently—for[n]example, July to June is the "Wheat Year," and October[n]to September is the "Sugar Year" or "Pesticide Year."

entries.speaker: BLOSSOM
entries.en: Known as "flower watching" in English, hanami is an[n]old Japanese tradition for viewing the cherry blossoms[n]and enjoying the arrival of spring.

entries.speaker: BLOSSOM
entries.en: The "flower" mentioned in traditional Japanese poetry[n]actually refers to the plum flower. It's said that cherry[n]blossoms overtook the usage during the Heian period.

entries.speaker: GOLDEN
entries.en: Golden Week is a holiday that typically spans[n]the end of April to the beginning of May and[n]includes Saturday and Sunday.

entries.speaker: GOLDEN
entries.en: The "Golden" part of the phrase came from the[n]Japanese broadcasting term "golden time," which[n]refers to the most desirable time slot of the day.

entries.speaker: MALAISE
entries.en: In Japan, the May Blues are named as such due to[n]the change of seasons and the number of people[n]who fall ill after the long holiday at April's end.

entries.speaker: MALAISE
entries.en: Similar terms are used across the world. Students in the[n]USA get the "September Blues" after summer vacation,[n]while the UK has the "January Blues" to contend with.

entries.speaker: GALLERY
entries.en: A room or corridor where artwork is on display. The[n]gallery is also the area where observers group together[n]for all sorts of events, from court to golf tournaments.

entries.speaker: GALLERY
entries.en: It can also refer to society at large—especially in regards[n]to the majority opinion—or even a passageway made by[n]an animal, such as the tunnel system of a mole.

entries.speaker: POLLENOSIS
entries.en: This is an allergic reaction that triggers when pollen[n]makes contact with membranes in the nose or eyes.[n]It primarily causes sneezing, runny nose, and itchiness.

entries.speaker: POLLENOSIS
entries.en: These symptoms came to rise whenever English[n]farmers harvested their pastures, leading the nickname[n]for pollenosis—hay fever—to become commonplace.

entries.speaker: JAPANESE
entries.en: In contrast to imported Western art styles, paintings[n]produced post-1900 using techniques developed[n]within Japan are referred to as "Nihonga."

entries.speaker: JAPANESE
entries.en: Foreigners visiting Japan during the Meiji period called[n]this "Japanese painting," which the literal Japanese[n]translate as "Nihon" (Japan) and "ga" (artwork).

entries.speaker: MASTER
entries.en: Most often used in the phrase, "master of the arts," it's[n]reserved for artists with incredible skill and techniques[n]that grew to be heavily influential in their mediums.

entries.speaker: MASTER
entries.en: One of the most prolific masters in painting, Pablo[n]Picasso, also has one of the longest full names in art[n]history: 103 letters total!

entries.speaker: CONFERENCE

entries.speaker: CONFERENCE

entries.speaker: WARDROBE
entries.en: In Japanese schools, students change their wardrobe[n]twice annually, in the summer and the winter, for[n]comfort's sake.

entries.speaker: WARDROBE
entries.en: It's said that the practice originated in China—during[n]the Edo Period, people were supposed to change their[n]wardrobes four times a year.

entries.speaker: CURRENCY
entries.en: Originating from the Latin word "currentia" ("flowing"),[n]this term applies specifically to money, no matter the[n]medium—though it does not include checks or credit.

entries.speaker: CURRENCY
